newsitem.title: USA: Jury selected for fourth Kevorkian trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury selected for fourth Kevorkian trial.

text.p: A jury of eight men and six women was seated on Tuesday for Jack Kevorkian's fourth assisted suicide trial after only one day of jury selection, setting the stage for opening arguments on Wednesday.

Kevorkian, 69, faces four felony charges including violating the state's unwritten "common law" banning physician-assisted suicide for his role in the Aug. 30, death of Loretta Peabody, who suffered from multiple sclerosis.
Kevorkian, who has admitted attending 45 deaths since 1990, also has been charged with practicing medicine without a license.
The retired pathologist was acquitted on assisted suicide charges once in 1994 and twice in 1996 in trials held in the Detroit area.

Ionia County Circuit Judge Charles Miel set a hearing for Wednesday to consider a request from Kevorkian's attorneys for a change of venue and a prosecution objection to Miel's decision to excuse the assisted suicide crusader from attending the proceedings.

Miel Monday agreed to excuse Kevorkian, but Ionia County Prosecutor Ray Voet objected at Tuesday's hearing and said the defendant must appear in court at least once to waive his right to attend the trial.
Kevorkian attorney Geoffrey Fieger told Miel Tuesday the retired pathologist would likely become impatient with the proceedings and could disrupt them.
Kevorkian, who previously said he was afraid of the "Nazi goons" in Ionia, was not at jury selection. Those who attended included Joe Peabody, the former husband of Loretta Peabody, and his new wife.
Questioning of jurors was held in a theatre, the only place in town large enough to hold the jury pool of about 150 people.
Miel excused more than 40 jurors before the final group was selected. People who were dismissed included those who said they had strong feelings either in favour of or against assisted suicide.
Fieger argued for the change of venue because he said Kevorkian could not get a fair trial in the conservative, west-central Michigan town of 7,000 because of excessive publicity.
He cited an advertisement placed by area doctors in the local newspaper on Monday opposing assisted suicide. One of the physicians was in the jury pool but was immediately dismissed.
About 15 people protesting assisted suicide, mostly members of Not Dead Yet, an organisation of disabled persons, demonstrated outside the theatre.
